analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated trust fund to pay for water and sewer repairs, funded by a higher corporate tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 5 Democratic cosponsors but never got a committee hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a permanent federal trust fund of up to $35 billion a year for water and sewer infrastructure, funded by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%. The money would pay for replacing lead pipes, cleaning up PFAS-contaminated wells, fixing school drinking water, upgrading treatment plants, and extending water service to tribes and border communities. It would also require states to direct at least half of their water revolving funds to grants that forgive loan repayment for disadvantaged communities, and allow public systems to use those funds to buy private water utilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing unaffordable water bills or shutoffs, residents of homes with lead service lines, schoolchildren drinking from old fixtures, families with PFAS-contaminated wells, tribal communities lacking safe water, and border-region colonias. Construction workers building these projects would benefit from prevailing wage and project labor agreement protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with lead pipes or unaffordable water bills

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Water Affordability, Transparency, Equity, and Reliability Trust Fund funded by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%, capped at $35 billion a year or one-twentieth of the EPA's 20-year water infrastructure need, whichever is larger [S3].

Directs the fund to lead pipe replacement grants for homeowners, PFAS treatment for public water systems and contaminated household wells, school drinking water infrastructure, tribal water and sewer facilities, and colonias water assistance [S3].

Requires states to use at least 50% of federal water revolving fund money for additional subsidization (loan forgiveness) where there are sufficient applications, shifting aid from loans toward grants for communities that struggle to repay [S3].

Directs EPA to study and report on water affordability, service disconnections, tax liens and foreclosures for unpaid water bills, and discriminatory practices in water service and state funding decisions [S3].
Preserves prevailing wage requirements and requires project labor agreements on water construction projects funded through the state revolving funds [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, through a 3.5 percentage point increase in the federal corporate income tax rate (21% to 24.5%), which funds the trust fund. The higher rate would apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2022 [S3]. Private water utility owners could also lose systems, since the bill allows public entities to use revolving funds to purchase privately owned water systems from a willing or unwilling seller [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations paying a higher income tax rate

drawbacks.text: The bill is paid for by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%, the first such increase since the 2017 tax law; opponents of higher corporate taxes argue this reduces business investment and falls partly on workers and savers over time [S3].

The bill requires states to maximize the use of project labor agreements on water projects, which nonunion contractors argue can raise bidding costs and restrict competition, a standard point of contention in infrastructure funding [S3].

The bill bars state revolving funds from financing projects that mainly serve new communities or subdivisions (except advanced decentralized wastewater systems), which developers of new housing could face as a constraint on growth-related infrastructure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a large, concrete benefit — a dedicated stream of up to $35 billion a year for water systems that currently depend on unpredictable annual appropriations — with the cost concentrated in a 3.5-point corporate tax increase. The main design tradeoffs are the project labor agreement mandate and restrictions on funding new-development infrastructure, and the trust fund's automatic appropriations would remove the annual congressional oversight that comes with normal budgeting. On balance, the benefits flow to households and communities while the cost falls on corporate taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2023, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Water Affordability, Transparency, Equity, and Reliability Act on March 22, 2023, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Wyden, Blumenthal, Merkley, Warren, and Welch [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind in the entire Congress [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor for a vote [S5].
No version of the bill was introduced in the House during the 118th Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations kept the 21% corporate tax rate instead of the proposed 24.5%, and private water utilities were never exposed to the bill's provision allowing public systems to purchase them. Households with lead pipes, contaminated wells, or unaffordable water bills received no relief from this bill, though separate 2021 infrastructure funding continued.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five Democratic cosponsors

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OR); Finance Committee chair and cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its Finance Committee chair, but his committee never held a hearing or markup on it

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats or the independent Sanders; no Republican signed on, and since the bill never got a vote there is no roll-call record of how the full Senate would have split.

industries.note: The bill would let municipalities use federal revolving funds to purchase privately owned water systems 'from a willing or unwilling seller,' effectively enabling condemnation-style buyouts that would shrink the private water industry. Customers of acquired systems would become users of publicly owned systems.

The bill's funding comes entirely from raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%, an estimated multi-billion-dollar annual cost. Public polling generally shows mixed views on corporate tax increases, with some support when tied to visible public goods.

Up to $35 billion a year in dedicated infrastructure spending creates a large construction market, with prevailing wage and project labor agreement requirements steering work toward union-scale contractors.

States would be barred from using revolving funds for projects that mainly benefit new communities or subdivisions, limiting access to subsidized sewer and water extensions for greenfield development (with an exception for advanced decentralized systems).
